extracted.intended_audience: general readers, students and researchers interested in emotions and social psychology
extracted.subtask_description: Summarizing and classifying the emotion 'embarrassment' including its definition, causes, types, physiological/behavioral markers, social functions, and specific forms (professional, vicarious). Useful for emotional taxonomy or social-psychology analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of embarrassment
rubrics_metrics.description: Embarrassment (or awkwardness) is an emotional state that is associated with mild to severe levels of discomfort, and which is usually experienced when someone commits (or thinks of) a socially unacceptable, or frowned-upon act that is witnessed by or revealed to others.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Frequently grouped with shame and guilt; considered a 'self-conscious emotion' and can have a profoundly negative impact on a person's thoughts or behavior. Usually involves some perception of loss of honor or dignity; level and type depend on the situation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Causes of embarrassment
rubrics_metrics.description: Embarrassment can be personal, caused by unwanted attention to private matters or personal flaws or mishaps or shyness. Some causes stem from personal actions (being caught in a lie, making a mistake) and many cultures find being seen nude or inappropriately dressed particularly stressful.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Personal embarrassment can also stem from actions of others (e.g., a parent showing baby pictures, derogatory comments, gossip, rejection, being made focus of attention, witnessing someone else's embarrassment). Context examples include birthday celebrants, newlyweds, etc.

rubrics_metrics.name: Physiological and behavioral responses to embarrassment
rubrics_metrics.description: Personal embarrassment is usually accompanied by some combination of blushing, sweating, nervousness, stammering, and fidgeting. Sometimes the embarrassed person tries to mask embarrassment with smiles or nervous laughter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Responses vary by culture (masking with laughter more common in some cultures). There may also be feelings of anger depending on perceived seriousness or intentionality by others. Range of responses: from perceiving the act as humorous to intense apprehension or fear.

rubrics_metrics.name: Social function — apology/appeasement (Goffman)
rubrics_metrics.description: Embarrassment may serve an apology or appeasement function: the embarrassed individual 'demonstrates that he/she is at least disturbed by the fact and may prove worthy at another time'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Empirical suggestion (Semin & Manstead) that appearing embarrassed after committing a social faux pas can increase likability of the perpetrator compared to appearing unconcerned, even without restitution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proneness to embarrassment as social regulator
rubrics_metrics.description: Proneness to embarrassment (concern for how one is evaluated by others) can act as a brake on behavior that would be dysfunctional for a group or culture.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evidence cited: individuals not prone to embarrassment are more likely to engage in antisocial behavior; adolescent boys who display more embarrassment were less likely to engage in aggressive/delinquent behaviors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Professional or official embarrassment
rubrics_metrics.description: Embarrassment can be professional or official, especially after statements expressing confidence in a stated course of action, or willful disregard for evidence. It increases in instances involving official duties, workplace facilities, large amounts of money/materials, or loss of human life.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: government's failed public policy, exposure of corrupt practices, celebrity scrutiny, exposure of falsified scientific data. Typical official responses include anger, denial, minimizing consequences, press statements, distancing from subordinates, or attempts to carry on as if nothing happened.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vicarious (second‑hand) embarrassment
rubrics_metrics.description: Vicarious embarrassment is an embarrassed feeling from observing the embarrassing actions of another person.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: People who rate themselves as more empathic are more likely to experience vicarious embarrassment. The effect occurs whether or not the observed party is aware; awareness generally increases strength, and accidental (vs intentional) actions also increase felt vicarious embarrassment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Six types of embarrassment (Sharkey & Stafford)
rubrics_metrics.description: A typology describing six types of embarrassment: Privacy violations; Lack of knowledge and skill; Criticism and rejection; Awkward acts; Appropriate image; Environment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Each type illustrated: Privacy violations (accidental exposure or invasion of space/information), Lack of knowledge/skill (forgetfulness, failure on easy tasks), Criticism/rejection (being center of attention positively or negatively), Awkward acts (inappropriate conversations, clumsiness, ungraceful actions), Appropriate image (body image, clothing, possessions), Environment (e.g., unexpected nudity in a movie with mixed company).

rubrics_metrics.name: Cupach & Metts typology: dimensions and four basic types
rubrics_metrics.description: Cupach and Metts discuss the dimensions intended–unintended and appropriate–inappropriate, yielding four basic types of embarrassing circumstances: Faux pas (socially awkward acts), Accidents, Mistakes, and Failure to perform a duty or moral obligation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This framework emphasizes whether actions were intended and whether they were appropriate, helping classify embarrassing events for analysis or intervention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Actor-responsible vs observer-responsible embarrassment
rubrics_metrics.description: Based on Cupach & Metts: two basic embarrassment situations are 'actor responsible' (the actor executes an act inappropriate to social norms, inconsistent with role expectations, or out of sync with social identity) and 'observer responsible' (an individual becomes the focus of attention through recognition, praise, criticism, correction, teasing, being tripped/bumped, or having information revealed publicly).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Actor-responsible focuses on the actor's mismatch with norms/roles/identity; observer-responsible focuses on processes that make a person the target of attention or disclosure. Useful for diagnosing cause and likely social reactions.
